articles.title: ‘I wanted to live’: A Ukrainian orphan’s journey through Russian occupation
articles.summary: Denys Kostev says he was forcibly transferred in 2022 and coerced into pro-Russian campaigns before finally escaping.
articles.body:
Kyiv, Ukraine – When the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began, Denys Kostev was 18 and living in an orphanage in Kherson. Appalled by the war, he used to film social media videos decrying the invading Russian forces.

But he was soon forcibly transferred to occupied Crimea, and his rhetoric suddenly went in the other direction.

Now in Kyiv four years later, Kostev told Al Jazeera he played the role of a poster child for wartime Russia just to survive.

Sprightly, eloquent and photogenic, he used to attend a theatre club at his orphanage in the southern Ukrainian city, where he lived after his mother’s incarceration and death.

The experience helped him “star” in numerous videos for Russian television networks – because refusing to be filmed meant risking physical assault or being threatened with jail, he said.

“It was useful to play this pro-Russian role,” said Kostev, who, having ultimately escaped Russia, is now preparing to fight for Ukraine. “I wanted to live.”

But surviving did not come easy, he said.

Tanks rolled into Kherson days after the war began. People suspected of pro-Ukrainian sympathies were rounded up and interrogated. Some were allegedly abused.

In late 2022, while at the orphanage, Kostev also studied in a trade school. But as the war intensified, he and others were relocated to the Luchisty (“Full of Sunshine”) summer camp in Russia-annexed Crimea.

“Every morning, you wake up to the Russian anthem, and every Monday, there’s a celebratory hoisting of the Russian flag,” Kostev said of his time there.

“They’re without parents, no one to explain what’s right or wrong,” he said. “At a certain point, you begin to repeat pro-Russian narratives.”

At least one teenager Kostev met in the camp enlisted to fight against Kyiv, he said.

Ukraine is working to return allegedly abducted children and collect evidence against individuals suspected of being involved in their capture. More than 2,600 children have returned so far.

The summer camp’s “administration” has not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Kyiv said that 84 Ukrainian orphans were held there in 2023.

Those who left were among almost 4,000 children forcibly taken from orphanages in Russia-occupied Ukrainian regions, according to Ukrainian rights groups. Kyiv claims that Moscow has herded almost 20,000 Ukrainian minors to Russia to “brainwash” them during the war.

While the Kremlin acknowledges that children are being “re-educated”, it rejects Ukraine’s claims, saying that any children who have been moved were rescued from war zones.

Some of these children lost parents during Russian shelling, and others ended up in “summer camps” after pro-Moscow authorities reportedly convinced their parents to let them go for “safety reasons”.

Ukraine claims that some children were abducted from parents who refused to collaborate with Moscow-installed “administrations” in Russia-occupied areas.

Russian forces and their Ukrainian collaborators have also been accused by Ukrainian rights groups of interrogating and abusing parents – and checking their bodies for pro-Kyiv tattoos or bruises left by recoiling firearms.

International rights groups decry the alleged abduction and indoctrination of children as one of the Kremlin’s gravest crimes.

“The physical destruction of this war is visible to everyone, but the campaign to abduct and ‘re-educate’ Ukrainian children as Russian represents something more sinister altogether,” Ivar Dale, a senior policy adviser with the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, a rights watchdog, told Al Jazeera.

“It’s unacceptable,” he said. “There are deeply disturbing reports that Russia is carrying out military indoctrination with a view to use some of these children in the armed forces in their war against Ukraine.”

Some 5,500 young Ukrainians in Russia-occupied areas were sent into Yunarmiya (“Young Army”), a movement that provides military training, according to Ukrainian officials.

The earlier the age, the deeper the transformation of a child’s worldview, according to Svitlana Chunikhina, vice president of the Association of Political Psychologists of Ukraine, a group in Kyiv.

“Children have a flexible psyche; they quickly adapt to a new environment, they mostly trust adults – sometimes involuntarily, but they have no other choice – and take many things for granted,” she said.

That is why they cannot resist Moscow’s narratives, she said.

“But it doesn’t mean that the same will surely happen to all Ukrainian children,” Chunikhina said.

While younger children studied in the camp according to the Russian curriculum, the education system did not appear to have had a thorough, comprehensive programme for teenagers such as Kostev.

Along with his friends, he hung around a Soviet-era compound dotted with cypresses, acacias and evergreen shrubs.

They were not allowed to leave it – but occasionally sneaked out to buy cigarettes and alcohol. Those who were caught drunk were isolated for three days in the hospital and were threatened with prison by the camp’s security chief, a former officer with Ukraine’s special forces who had switched sides, said Kostev, who is now 22.

The idea that the children would “never return to Ukraine” was drummed into them, he said.

In April 2023, after months in camps in Crimea, Kostev was sent back to the occupied southern town of Henichesk – and learned that Russian troops had withdrawn from Kherson seven months earlier.

He enrolled in another trade school and was housed in a squalid, ice-cold dormitory he complained about in a video that went viral.

The next morning, Russia-installed police strip-searched him, claiming he was “spying” for Kyiv and threatened him with jail, he said.

Then he was forced to extol Russia on camera.

In one video, he said he had joined a Kremlin-funded youth movement, wrapped himself in a Russian flag and declared that he wanted to enlist.

But he told Al Jazeera that he was forced and coerced into championing Russia, and had always wanted to leave.

In early 2024, Kostev got in touch with his elder brother and grandmother who had relocated to Germany. He managed to join them and later crossed into Poland, where he spent months awaiting a new Ukrainian passport.

In April, he returned to Ukraine. He said he has attended a military training camp and is now in the early stages of his military career as a drone pilot.

“Wherever you are – home is better,” he said, sitting in a shopping mall in a Kyiv suburb, shortly before air raid sirens forced everyone outside.

articles.title: 'Lost' medieval castle found hiding in plain sight after professor spots telltale clues
articles.summary: A University College Dublin professor found that up to 80% of the medieval Roebuck Castle is still intact beneath Victorian plaster on the modern campus.
articles.body: A professor recently discovered that a medieval castle thought to have been lost for centuries was hiding in plain sight — inside a Victorian-era building on a modern college campus. The discovery was announced by University College Dublin (UCD), in Dublin, Ireland, on Sept. 18. The school announced in a release — entitled "'Lost' medieval castle found hiding inside UCD building" — that medieval archaeology professor Tadhg O'Keeffe found substantial portions of the medieval Roebuck Castle still survive within the university's present-day building. DISCOVERY BENEATH SOCCER FIELD REVEALS MASSIVE MEDIEVAL CONVENT LOST FOR CENTURIES The present-day Roebuck Castle retained the name of its medieval predecessor — but the Victorian-looking building was long believed to contain little, if any, of the original castle. The original structure had fallen into ruin by the 18th century and was later incorporated into a residence that underwent extensive alterations, including a major Victorian makeover in 1874. UCD purchased the property in 1986. O'Keeffe told Fox News Digital that, despite those centuries of changes, most of the medieval structure is still there. "I would say that 70 to 80% of the building is still there, hidden under Victorian plaster," he said. He began investigating after studying 18th-century watercolors by artist Gabriel Beranger, which depicted the medieval castle before the property underwent major redevelopment. 1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER "I wasn't terribly optimistic," O'Keeffe said. "When I got into the building and had a look around, I realized that actually, most of the castle is still there, inside the building. "It's not obvious to the naked eye," he continued. "It's not obvious to a non-expert. But I specialize in medieval castle architecture, and I saw all the indications when I went in that the castle is still there." The clues were hiding beneath the building's more modern appearance. O'Keeffe pointed to unusually thick walls, along with a stone vault and arched stone roof, as evidence of the building's medieval past. "The gate tower is very clear on the inside," he said. FIRST-EVER IMAGES REVEAL MYSTERIOUS REMAINS OF TOWN SWALLOWED BY SEA 700 YEARS AGO "Everything is plastered over so you can't see the original stonework anymore, but it's all clearly still there," he said. "Also, the windows are splayed, and splayed windows are a real indication of a medieval date." Roebuck Castle was likely built in the early 13th century, after the Norman invasion of Ireland began in the late 12th century. Roebuck Castle also stands out for another reason: Researchers know who owned it through much of the Middle Ages. The owners were "people of some significance," O'Keeffe added. HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR "One of them, in modern terms, would be the equivalent of the chief justice in the Supreme Court, the most senior legal person in Ireland for part of the Middle Ages," the historian said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Another resident at one stage, temporarily, was King James II. It's reputed that he lived there briefly in the late 1600s." That level of detail is unusual, O'Keeffe said, because records for castles around Dublin are generally sparse. "The great takeaway ... is never assume things are gone." "We have a record of its owners really until about the start of the 17th century, when it seems to have been abandoned and probably suffered in the wars of the mid-17th century," he said. "So it's unusual for a castle of its type to have a recorded history." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Although the renovations preserved much of the medieval castle, O'Keeffe said, it appears to have been more a matter of practicality than historic preservation. "There was no policy of preservation. There was not a particular interest in the medieval building," he said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "They clearly figured that the fastest way to do that was to simply leave those walls and incorporate them." O'Keeffe said the discovery suggests other castles in Ireland that are presumed lost could still survive within later buildings. "The great takeaway ... is never assume things are gone," he said. "You have to go in and look. You have to explore." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "There are probably lots of other castles that are locked up in buildings around the country [and] are assumed to be gone — but are not gone at all," he said.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer raises explosive doubt over who killed her children
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington argued for the first time that prosecutors failed to prove she killed her three children.
articles.body: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer made a surprise shift in strategy Tuesday, according to legal analysts — shifting gears from his argument at trial that she was not criminally responsible because she suffered from postpartum psychosis. "Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday. "Where is the evidence she did this?" Reddington made the argument while asking Sullivan to enter a not guilty finding after the jury deadlocked. LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR ASKS FOR ONE THING IN NEW VIDEO AFTER MISTRIAL DRAMA "I submit to the court there is no evidence she made any statements, as far as the actual killing of the children, which forms the basis of the indictments," Reddington said. Plymouth County prosecutors countered, calling his assertion "a laughable argument." But it marked a striking change in the way he's argued the case in the past. WATCH: Kevin Reddington spends 8 minutes, 27 seconds attacking the allegation that Lindsay Clancy killed her kids He pointed to what he described as gaps in the physical evidence, including the blood, DNA, timing and circumstances surrounding Clancy’s suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed. LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON SIGNALS HE'S OPEN TO A DEAL, HOPES DA WILL 'REVISIT' CASE "For the first time, we saw Kevin Reddington say that there’s reasonable doubt as to whether Lindsay Clancy actually killed her children," said former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani, who has been closely following the case. "He's never said that in the courtroom, outside the courtroom — and in fact at the beginning of the first trial, he offered to stipulate to Lindsay killing her three children." Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a verdict following roughly a week of deliberations. Since then, several jurors have spoken out publicly, describing an 11-1 deadlock with only one man voting to find her guilty of murder. LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS The 11 sided with Reddington's not guilty due to mental illness or defect defense. He argued that Clancy was not criminally responsible for strangling her children with exercise bands due to postpartum psychosis. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Only one juror voted to convict, and Reddington started calling him an "obstructionist" — first last week when approached by Fox News Digital and again outside the courthouse Tuesday. During the hearing, Reddington also raised concerns about the prosecution’s case and the police investigation launched after Clancy was found in the backyard suffering from injuries that left her paralyzed. LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS FACE DILEMMA: RETRIAL OR PLEA DEAL IN CASE INVOLVING 3 STRANGLED CHILDREN SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS "This may just be a defense lawyer denying everything, using the kitchen sink approach, hoping one of these arguments would resonate with Judge Sullivan," Rahmani said. "Or it could be a shift in defense strategy, where maybe instead of arguing insanity or lack of criminal responsibility at the retrial, they put on a third party culpability defense as well, arguing that maybe someone else is the real killer." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Reddington's comments came during oral arguments on what's called a Rule 25(b)(2) motion — asking Sullivan to override the deadlocked jury and enter a not-guilty finding on the alleged grounds that the Commonwealth's evidence was legally insufficient to garner a conviction. LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT Such motions are routine but seldom successful, according to Carol Erskine, a retired Massachusetts judge and child welfare advocate who has been following the case closely. LINDSAY CLANCY DA RARELY DOES PLEA DEALS, BUT HER CASE COULD BE THE 'EXCEPTION,' VETERAN ATTORNEY SAYS GOT A TIP? "He is arguing that [they] did not prove each and every element as required by law," she told Fox News Digital. "I understand why people don’t get this, but he had to argue sufficiency of evidence under Rule 25(b)(2) case law. He told the judge he asked for a Bowden instruction and was denied, which meant he was challenging the poor investigation/search at the home by police. It’s a very nuanced argument." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST It's also a different argument than the prior Rule 25 motion that Reddington filed at the end of Clancy's mistrial, which Sullivan denied. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "I will say it was a total surprise that his strategy changed from the original 25(b)(2) motion," Erskine said. "Did not expect it." LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW Clancy is due back in court on Nov. 2 for another motion hearing. She has pending motions to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds and to open an inquiry into the holdout juror. articles.title: A $450M art collection is poised to break Van Gogh and Cézanne’s auction records
articles.summary: In London, Sothebys unveiled works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, not seen for half a century, that could make for a historic night when they go under the hammer in the fall in New York.
articles.body: In New York this fall, Sotheby’s will put up for auction a rare Vincent van Gogh painting, not seen for half a century, which it expects will sell for a staggering $180 million and set a new auction record. That would normally be enough buzz for a marquee November evening sale — but there’s more. The auction house will also follow it up with a rare Paul Cézanne painting (also not seen for the last five decades), that it has estimated “in the region” of $120 million and hope will set a second record for the night. The two masterworks have both been held by the same family since the 1970s — and will sell alongside ten of their other collected artworks including a Monet and a Renoir, that together, Sotheby’s is promoting as the “El Dorado” of private art collections. If all goes as planned, the auction house will clean up $450 million (or more) in less than an hour. “It’s one of the greatest remaining collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art in private hands,” said Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe, who also referred to the group of artworks as “a mini Musée d’Orsay.” “It had this legendary, mythical status as one of the greats,” she said. “But now there is the reveal, and people will get the chance to see what it comprises.” Philip Hook, a former senior director at Sotheby’s said the mystery of the collection was a “constant” throughout his career. “What was in it? How good was it? The thing was, no one really knew,” Hook told journalists at a press view in London on Wednesday morning. One reason was because the Blaquier-Arrieta family never lent the pictures to museums, he said. The other was because they were based in Argentina. “This seemed a very, very long way away” in the ‘90s and noughties, he continued. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, owned by the late Argentinian businessman Carlos Pedro Blaquier and the art patron Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, is the latest mega-collector sell-off that the art market has relied on for the past few seasons to buoy its sales. It follows the collections of media magnate SI Newhouse, Microsoft founder Paul G Allen, socialite and art patron Pauline Karpidas, and Estée Lauder heir Leonard A. Lauder — the last of which included the $236 million Klimt that became the second-most expensive work of art to ever sell at auction. The lots are being sold by the children of the Blaquier-Arrieta family after Nelly’s death in 2020 and Carlos’ in 2023. Blaquier was president of a sugar mill, and Nelly served on international committees for major museums, and guided their collection. They were one of the most powerful families in Argentina. But for the last decade of Blaquier’s life, he was investigated for crimes against humanity, for allegedly detaining activists during the Argentina’s brutal military dictatorship from 1976-83, which the BBC reported that he denied. He never stood trial before his death, according to his obituary in La Nacion. A spokesperson for Sothebys said that he was never convicted and always maintained his innocence. While the upcoming sale will take place in New York, a handful of the 12 works –– including “En Canot (Jeune fille à la barque)” (1877) by Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Camille Pissarro’s “La Place du Théâtre-Français et l’avenue de l’Opéra, soleil d’après-midi en hiver” (1898) –– were unveiled together for the first time in London on Wednesday morning. That’s where the Blaquiers procured much of their collection, traveling during the summer months to purchase directly from Lefevre Gallery, a major player in Impressionist and Modern art until its closure at the turn of the 21st century. If both top lots set new records, it will be the second time both artist’s records have been broken in the same night, as part of the same collection. Christie’s historic 2022 sale of Paul Allen’s works led to the $117 million sale of Van Gogh’s landscape “Verger avec cyprès” and $137.7 million sale of Cézanne’s mountain scene “La Montagne Sainte-Victoire,” both painted in 1888. This Van Gogh painting, titled “Chataignier en fleurs roses et blanches,” which was not on show in London but instead on its way to Hong Kong where it will be displayed ahead of the auction later this year, was made in the last two months of the artist’s life in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise. Van Gogh had only just been released from the psychiatric facility in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he’d voluntarily admitted himself for a year, and Sotheby’s notes the “vigor” and “optimism” of the period. “It’s an amazing, exuberant palette,” Newman said, noting that there’s only a “handful” of works still out there from the end of the artist’s life. Several hang in the Musée d’Orsay, including one of his portraits of the physician who treated him, Doctor Paul Gachet. The neighboring Cézanne work, “Arlequin,” a vibrant color-clashing work that took centerstage in Sotheby’s London gallery, is from a set of four Harlequin paintings, and is the only one not held by a museum, the press release noted. It passed through the hands of important French art dealers Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg, and exhibited in seminal Cézanne exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Tate in London and the Art Institute of Chicago before it was eventually sold to the Blaquier family in 1975. Now, their collection is being marketed as one of the last great tranches of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art — a period of art that has become a safety net during economic turbulence. How the health of the art market at its highest end will fare as these collections dwindle remains to be seen. Newman acknowledged that it is a generational shift as collections that formed from the 1960s-80s come to market now as their owners age and pass. For the — very few — collectors in the world who can afford their own museum-worthy collection, Newman says this is a rare opportunity. “It’s a moment for those collectors, both established and new, to be competing, and that will be very interesting for us all to see.”

articles.title: US military completes withdrawal of troops from Iraq after 12-year mission
articles.summary: The U.S. military completed its withdrawal from Erbil Air Base, ending Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq while relocating its headquarters to Jordan.
articles.body: The U.S. military has completed the withdrawal of American forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base in Iraq, ending its Operation Inherent Resolve mission, U.S. Central Command announced Wednesday. The departure closes the Iraq chapter of the U.S.-led military mission launched against ISIS in 2014, while shifting primary responsibility for the country's security to Iraqi forces. The broader counter-ISIS campaign is not ending, however, with the U.S.-led task force relocating its headquarters to Jordan and operations continuing in Syria. "Job well done to the tens of thousands of American service members, diplomats, and civilian personnel who answered the call in Iraq," CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said. US SERVICE MEMBER KILLED IN IRAQ AS TROOPS RECOVER UNIDENTIFIED REMAINS IN JORDAN: CENTCOM "Because of your grit, sacrifice and professionalism, ISIS no longer poses a systemic threat to Iraq’s national security and Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, now possess the capacity, leadership, and operational independence to unilaterally manage threats to their homeland," Cooper said. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the departure the formal conclusion of Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq and said it marked a transition "from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship." MOTORCYCLE PATROLS IRANIAN CITIES, CHECKPOINTS RISE AS REGIME BRACES FOR UNREST The Pentagon said the U.S. will continue providing targeted training and intelligence support to Iraqi forces even after the withdrawal, while Iraqi security forces, including the Peshmerga, take the lead in keeping ISIS remnants suppressed. Erbil Air Base in northern Iraq served as the main operational hub for Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve and hosted most of the roughly 1,500 American and coalition forces supporting counter-ISIS operations, according to CENTCOM. U.S. and coalition forces began leaving federal Iraq last October as Washington and Baghdad moved toward a bilateral defense relationship. The final removal of personnel and equipment from Erbil completed that transition on Sept. 30. The withdrawal followed an agreement reached between Washington and Baghdad under the Biden administration in 2024 and carried forward under the Trump administration. Combined Joint Task Force — Operation Inherent Resolve remains active and is now headquartered in Jordan, according to CENTCOM. U.S. forces also continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria alongside coalition partners and the Syrian government. SYRIA OFF US TERROR BLACKLIST AFTER NEARLY 50 YEARS AS TRUMP ADMIN CLEARS INVESTMENT HURDLE The U.S. has roughly 4,000 troops stationed in Jordan, where American forces will continue monitoring the ISIS threat. Muwaffaq Salti Air Base hosts U.S. combat aircraft and has itself become a target during the conflict with Iran. Three U.S. service members were killed in an Iranian attack on the base in July. "As we step back and hand full primary responsibility for Iraq’s security to the Government of Iraq and the brave people of Iraq, U.S. and coalition forces stationed across the region will remain ready to respond to any ISIS threats that arise," Cooper said. "Maintaining our vigilance and readiness is essential to protecting the U.S. homeland and strengthening regional security," he added. The withdrawal ends a U.S. military presence in Iraq that was reestablished in 2014, when Iraqi authorities sought international assistance as ISIS captured large areas of the country. U.S. troops had previously left Iraq in 2011 following the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. For the last several years, roughly 2,500 U.S. troops have been stationed in Iraq. The majority departed last year, leaving hundreds of troops in the northern Kurdish region until the final withdrawal. The final departure comes as Iraq faces a separate security challenge from powerful Iran-backed militias operating inside the country. Baghdad has sought to bring weapons held by non-state groups under government control, but some of the most influential militias have resisted disarming. IRANIAN PRESIDENT BLAMES US FOR MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT WHILE DENYING NUCLEAR AMBITIONS, OFFERS TO DILUTE URANIUM The Pentagon explicitly identified those militias as one of the security challenges Baghdad will now be expected to confront. "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including ISIS remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the Government of Iraq," Parnell said. The withdrawal also reduces the number of U.S. military targets inside Iraq after American forces there faced repeated attacks by Iran-aligned groups following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. During this year's war with Iran, seven of the 18 U.S. service members killed in Iranian attacks were killed in Iraq, according to Fox News reporting. The withdrawal has drawn sharply different reactions inside Iraq. Iran-aligned groups celebrated the U.S. departure, while officials in the country's Kurdish region have raised concerns about the loss of American air-defense capabilities amid drone and missile threats. Kurdish officials say their region has faced more than 1,000 Iranian drone and ballistic missile attacks since the war with Iran began Feb. 28, adding to concerns over the removal of U.S. forces and air-defense capabilities. Thousands of ISIS fighters also remain in Iraq and Syria despite the collapse of the terror group's organized military threat. The Iraqi government has said its forces will continue operations against ISIS, while the Pentagon said the U.S. remains committed to preventing the group from reconstituting from Iraqi territory. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP CENTCOM said U.S. and coalition forces elsewhere in the region will remain prepared to respond if ISIS again poses a threat. "The United States supports a strong sovereign Iraq that secures its borders, protects its people, and serves as the foundation for deeper commercial, diplomatic, and security cooperation between our two countries," Parnell said. Fox News' Liz Friden and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: US to double EB-5 visa fees from November 30: What it means for Indian investors seeking green card
articles.summary: The US is sharply increasing fees for its EB-5 immigrant investor programme, raising the cost for foreign nationals seeking a Green Card through
articles.body: The US is sharply increasing fees for its EB-5 immigrant investor programme, raising the cost for foreign nationals seeking a Green Card through investment. The new fee structure, finalised by US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), takes effect on November 30.For Indian investors, the change means thousands of dollars in additional government filing costs at a time when demand for the EB-5 route has risen sharply. The higher fees, however, do not change the amount of capital an investor must invest in a qualifying US project.The fee for Form I-526, used by standalone investors, will rise from USD 3,675 to USD 7,615. For investors applying through a USCIS-approved regional centre, the initial Form I-526E fee will increase from USD 3,675 to USD 7,850, news agency PTI reported.Both initial petitions will also carry a USD 75 technology fee, while regional-centre investors will have to pay a separate investor integrity fee. The fee for Form I-829, used to remove conditions on permanent resident status, will rise from USD 3,750 to USD 5,000.What is the US EB-5 Immigrant Investor Programme?Created by the US Congress in 1990, the US EB-5 Immigrant Investor Programme allows foreign investors and their immediate families to seek permanent residency, or a Green Card, by investing in a US commercial enterprise and creating at least 10 full-time jobs for American workers. Applicants must invest USD 1.05 million in a qualifying business or USD 800,000 in a Targeted Employment Area or infrastructure project.The minimum investment is currently USD 1.05 million for a qualifying business. The threshold falls to USD 800,000 when the investment is made in a Targeted Employment Area (TEA) or an eligible infrastructure project.Applicants can invest as standalone investors or through a USCIS-approved regional centre. If the requirements are met, the investor, their spouse and qualifying children can seek Green Cards.How much will EB-5 fees increase?The biggest increase affects the initial petitions used to begin the EB-5 process.For standalone investors, the Form I-526 filing fee will more than double from USD 3,675 to USD 7,615, an increase of USD 3,940.For investors applying through an approved regional centre, the initial Form I-526E fee will rise from USD 3,675 to USD 7,850, an increase of USD 4,175.The fee for Form I-829 will increase from USD 3,750 to USD 5,000.Regional centres themselves will face much larger increases. The fee for an initial Form I-956 application seeking regional-centre designation will rise from USD 17,795 to USD 44,115, while Form I-956F will increase from USD 17,795 to USD 42,675. The annual Form I-956G fee, however, will fall from USD 3,035 to USD 2,165.What should Indian EB-5 applicants know?For Indians considering the programme, the key changes are:Initial standalone investor fee: USD 3,675 → USD 7,615Initial regional-centre investor fee: USD 3,675 → $7,850I-829 fee: USD 3,750 → USD 5,000Minimum investment: remains USD 800,000 for qualifying TEA/infrastructure projects andUSD 1.05 millionfor other qualifying investmentsJob requirement: at least 10 qualifying full-time jobsEffective date of new fees: November 30, 2026Visa availability: remains subject to annual and country-specific limitsThe fee increase therefore does not change the underlying EB-5 investment requirement. It makes the application process more expensive for Indian investors, while the separate questions of investment risk, project eligibility and Green Card availability remain.For an Indian investor using the regional-centre route, the initial USCIS filing fee alone will be USD 4,175 higher from November 30. The new fees are in addition to the investment capital itself and other expenses such as legal and project-related costs.Why are more Indians looking at EB-5?The higher charges come as the EB-5 route has attracted growing interest from Indian nationals, particularly those facing lengthy waits in other employment-based immigration categories.According to data cited by The American Bazaar, EB-5 filings from India rose from around 75 in fiscal year 2022 to nearly 1,900 in fiscal year 2025, an increase of roughly 25 times over three years.The programme has also attracted interest among Indians already living in the US on temporary visas such as H-1B and F-1, who may be looking for an alternative route towards permanent residency.However, Indian applicants should note that paying the higher EB-5 fees does not guarantee an immediate Green Card. EB-5 visas remain subject to annual and country-specific limits, and demand from India has resulted in visa availability constraints in the unreserved category.Why is the US raising EB-5 fees?USCIS said the agency is largely funded through the fees it charges rather than taxes.The agency said the fees cover the cost of reviewing applications, conducting background checks, verifying eligibility, detecting fraud and maintaining programme operations.The new fee structure therefore increases the administrative cost of pursuing an EB-5 Green Card, but does not change the programme's underlying investment thresholds.Will the fee hike affect the Green Card wait for Indians?The fee increase itself does not change the number of EB-5 visas available or remove country-specific limits.For Indian applicants, the Green Card timeline will continue to depend on visa availability, the applicant's EB-5 category, and the number of applications being processed.This makes the distinction between application cost and visa availability important. Indian investors will pay substantially more to file under the new fee structure, but the higher payment does not by itself provide faster Green Card processing or additional visa availability.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gentle giant ‘Backpack’ declared winner of Alaska’s Fat Bear Week
articles.summary: After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear of Alaska’s Katmai National Park and Preserve.
articles.body: After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear of Alaska’s Katmai National Park and Preserve. The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced Tuesday that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, won with more than 100,000 votes, narrowly beating Bear 910 with just over 50% of the poll. The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state’s southwest corner toward the Aleutian Islands. Fat Bear Week was started in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies. Last year’s winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — clinched his victory at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was handily defeated in the first round of competition this year by Bucky, who went on to lose a faceoff against Backpack, known officially as Bear 89. The event this year featured 16 bears vying for the heavyweight title in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament. All voting is done online at and the winner was declared Tuesday evening after the final poll closed. The public could watch the bears on explore.org’s livestream cameras before deciding on their favorite. “Fat bears are successful bears,” the nonprofit says on its website. This group gorges itself on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River starting in late June. It’s there that they can stuff themselves to accumulate the fat reserves they will need to survive the winter. To be featured in the contest, the bears must frequent the area around the river. Backpack is the son of former Fat Bear Week champion Holly, who introduced him to the Brooks River when he was a first-year cub in 2006. His name was inspired by his habit of climbing onto his mother’s back when they swam the river. This year’s fans cheered on Backpack in the contest’s Instagram comments, noting his lineage and reputation as a gentle giant. “Unlike many large adult male bears, Backpack hasn’t shown much aggression toward his competitors,” his contestant profile reads. Backpack uses his “quiet strength” rather than brawling and is often seen in wildlife cameras sitting on a rock downstream, appearing to take in the scenery around him. He defeated Bear 910, who is also the daughter of a former champion: 409 Beadnose. Adult male brown bears typically weigh 600 to 900 pounds (about 270 to 410 kilograms) in midsummer. By the time they are ready to hibernate after feasting on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh well over 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Females are about one-third smaller. The bears may each eat as many as 30 fish a day this time of year, working hard to eat a year’s worth of food in about six months. During winter hibernation, the bears do not eat or drink and can lose one-third of their body weight. Fat Bear Week’s contestants also included five bear families, in recognition of the record high number of families and cubs at the river this summer. A mother must feed and protect her cubs while also eating enough calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs often face the risk of attack by other bears due to territorialism or food scarcity. Bear 132 and her three spring cubs advanced to the semifinals, but lost out to Bear 910. Bear 132 has become one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River, according to her contestant profile. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days, wandering the river corridor alone. They were reunited a few days later.

articles.title: Ex-NFL star Antonio Brown set to appear in Miami court for expected plea agreement
articles.summary: Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown is scheduled to be in a Miami courtroom Wednesday to accept a plea deal that will let him avoid prison time on a reduced charge in an attempted murder case, according to his attorney.
articles.body: MIAMI — Former NFL star wide receiver Antonio Brown is scheduled to be in a Miami courtroom Wednesday to accept a plea deal that will let him avoid prison time on a reduced charge in an attempted murder case, according to his attorney. Defense attorney Mark Eiglarsh has said Brown will plead no contest to aggravated assault and be sentenced to probation. He also said adjudication will be withheld, meaning Brown will not be considered a convicted felon. Brown could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original charge. Eiglarsh has said the agreement with prosecutors was too good to turn down. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office said previously that details would be clarified at the hearing. Brown is accused of grabbing a handgun from a security staffer after a celebrity boxing match in Miami on May 16, 2025, and firing two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier, according to an arrest warrant. Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu told investigators that one of the bullets grazed his neck. Brown has said on social media that he was defending himself from an attack and others were trying to steal jewelry from him. Florida’s Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat. Richard Cooper, an attorney for Nantambu, has called the plea deal a fair one. He has said Nantambu forgives Brown and would not cooperate with law enforcement. Brown, 38, spent 12 years in the NFL and was an All-Pro wide receiver who last played in 2021 for Tampa Bay, including winning a Super Bowl with quarterback Tom Brady. Over the course of his career, much of it spent with Pittsburgh, he had 928 receptions for more than 12,000 yards and accounted for 88 total touchdowns, including punt returns and one pass. During a 2021 game with Tampa Bay against the New York Jets, Brown took off his jersey, shoulder pads and gloves and ran off the field, leading to his release by the Buccaneers and effectively ending his career. Brown has dealt with several legal problems over the years. He previously was accused of battery of a moving truck driver, several domestic violence charges, failure to pay child support and other incidents. Brown was extradited in November 2025 from Dubai, where he has business interests, after an arrest warrant on the attempted murder charge was issued in June of the same year.

articles.title: Car given for servicing, dealer took it to another service centre where it crashed; see how the owner won Rs 4.25 lakh payout
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal state consumer commission has directed a car dealer and insurer to compensate a customer after his Renault Duster met with an
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The West Bengal state consumer commission has directed a car dealer and insurer to compensate a customer after his Renault Duster met with an accident while it was in the dealer's custody for servicing. The commission held that the dealer had no explanation for why the vehicle was being driven from Kharagpur towards Haldia and set aside the insurer's rejection of the claim. The order was passed on September 29, 2026.Why did the customer approach the commission?According to the commission order, Rajesh Dubey bought the Renault Duster for Rs 15,23,736 on April 27, 2017. He insured it for the period from April 26, 2017, to April 25, 2018, with an insured declared value of about Rs 12.87 lakh.On March 2, 2018, the complainant handed over the vehicle to the authorised dealer for periodic servicing and repairs to minor scratches. On March 16, he was informed by police that the vehicle had met with an accident while travelling from Mecheda towards Haldia. The FIR recorded that it had collided with the rear of a trailer that had allegedly stopped suddenly. The collision caused substantial damage and the person driving the vehicle died.Dubey alleged that he had neither authorised nor known about the vehicle being taken from the dealer's premises towards Haldia. He sought an insurance claim, but the insurer later denied it, citing delay and discrepancies in workshop records.Why did the commission hold the dealer responsible?The bench of judicial member Rajes Guha Ray and member Santanu Saha noted that the dealer's own defence contained an admission that after repairs, the vehicle was being taken from its Kharagpur workshop towards its Haldia branch when it met with the accident.It said the dealer had a duty to take reasonable care of the vehicle while it was in its custody and could not use it beyond the purpose authorised by the owner.“The dealer has not explained why a vehicle entrusted for servicing was being driven from Kharagpur towards Haldia. No document establishing the complainant’s consent to that movement has been produced,” the commission noted.It rejected the dealer's reliance on a workshop clause permitting test driving. The commission said such a clause could not be treated as an unrestricted permission to take the customer's vehicle on an unexplained journey. It also held that insurance coverage did not remove the dealer's duty of care.The commission therefore held the dealer and its branch manager guilty of deficiency in service and made them responsible for the uninsured part of the proven physical loss, besides harassment and loss of use.The insurer had argued that the accident was reported about 25 days later and that the delay breached the policy conditions. The commission, however, noted that the accident had been reported to police and the damaged vehicle remained available for inspection.It said the insurer should have appointed a surveyor, examined the police and workshop records and assessed whether the vehicle had suffered partial, total or constructive total loss.“Repudiating the claim without undertaking that exercise was arbitrary and constituted deficiency in service,” the commission further held.It therefore set aside the repudiation of the insurance claim.The commission said the exact physical loss could not be determined without an independent assessment. It directed the insurer to appoint a licensed surveyor within 15 days. The surveyor must assess the damage and submit a report within 45 days.The insurer must then pay the policy-admissible amount within 30 days of receiving the survey report, with 9 percent annual interest from April 4, 2019. The dealer must pay any balance between the assessed loss and the amount payable by the insurer, subject to the limits specified in the order.Apart from the vehicle damage claim, the commission ordered:Rs 3 lakh compensation and Rs 50,000 litigation costs against the dealer and its branch manager.Rs 50,000 compensation and Rs 25,000 litigation costs against the insurer.These amounts will carry 9 percent annual interest if not paid within 45 days.Thus, the fixed compensation and litigation costs total Rs 4.25 lakh, apart from the insurance payout and any amount payable by the dealer towards the assessed vehicle loss.

articles.title: In hope of future revival, Mumbai family spent Rs 50 lakh keeping man’s body frozen since 2022
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Deeply disturbed by the death of an 80-year-old family member, his wife and two adult children preserved his body for four years, spending more
articles.body: MUMBAI: Deeply disturbed by the death of an 80-year-old family member, his wife and two adult children preserved his body for four years, spending more than Rs 50 lakh and researching whether it could eventually be sent to a cryonics facility in the US, police said.The unusual arrangement came to light on Monday night after Kurar police received a tip-off and visited a polyclinic in Malad. The man’s body was found inside a freezer at the premises, where the family had kept it after their residential building went into redevelopment.The man died in 2022 after suffering from cancer, kidney failure and other age-related ailments. His family initially kept his body in a freezer at their Malad home. When redevelopment work began at the building, they moved it to the clinic, police said.According to police, the family told investigators that they had been deeply affected by his death and could not bring themselves to perform his last rites. His wife and two adult children, including a lawyer daughter, had researched cryonics online and contacted organisations in the US that offer long-term preservation of people after legal death.The family was also consulting lawyers in India to understand the legalities involved in preserving the body and was exploring whether it could be transported to a facility in the US. Police said the family had spent more than Rs 50 lakh on preserving the body over the past four years.Hope of revivalThe family’s research centred on the possibility of preserving the man’s body in the hope that advances in future science could one day make revival possible, police said.Private cryonics organisations in the US offer to preserve legally dead people at extremely low temperatures, typically around -196°C using liquid nitrogen. The process involves preparing the body for long-term storage after legal death and transporting it to a specialised facility.Such organisations describe their objective as extending the possibility of future revival by preserving the body until technologies that could potentially reverse the damage caused by death become available. However, cryonics remains experimental and there is currently no established method of reviving a person preserved in this manner.Preservation packages offered by US-based organisations can cost tens of thousands of dollars, with some facilities quoting one-time costs of more than $28,000 and others charging up to about $45,000, depending on the services and type of preservation.The family had been exploring these options while simultaneously seeking legal advice in India, police said.Body found at clinicThe body remained at the Malad clinic even though the premises had been shut for about a month for renovation. Police said neither the clinic management nor the property owner had been informed that the body was being kept there.Relatives and neighbours, however, were aware of the arrangement, according to police.After questioning the family members, clinic management and the property owner, police ruled out foul play and said the man had died of natural causes. The family also produced documents relating to his death, police said.Cryopreservation—the preservation of cells, tissues or embryos at extremely low temperatures—is an established scientific technique in certain medical and research settings. Cryonics, by contrast, refers to preserving legally dead people with the hope that future technology may eventually make revival possible and remains an experimental practice.Police have not registered a case so far and are consulting experts on the legal aspects of keeping a human body preserved for such a prolonged period.Personnel have been deployed at the clinic while the family decides whether to proceed with its plan to send the body to a facility abroad or perform the last rites.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.body: In today’s newsletter: Rape allegations at Cornell University put New York laws in the spotlight. Palestinian family attacked during their attempt to return to the West Bank. And an exclusive look at Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs’ cushy prison accommodations. Here’s what to know today. Cornell rape allegations spotlight stringent New York state laws that have long drawn criticism New York state laws about consent and sexual assault are drawing national attention after prosecutors reopened the case of a former Cornell University student who alleges fraternity members raped her in 2024. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The law defines “mentally incapacitated” as victims being rendered temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct due to the influence of alcohol or drugs given to them without their consent. Defending his previous decision to not seek criminal charges, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said the former student “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” Some legal experts say the law effectively sets a higher bar for prosecutors and advocates have lobbied for changes in recent years. In states like California and Virginia, victims do not have to be given drugs or alcohol without their consent to be considered mentally incapacitated. Read the full story here. EXCLUSIVE: Diddy’s pampered life in prison includes massages, nude photos and Hennessy As Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs serves a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses, sources inside New Jersey’s Fort Dix federal prison tell NBC News the disgraced hip-hop mogul is still living a privileged life. Multiple sources say Combs uses a contraband phone to scroll Instagram and scan sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. Other inmates cook and clean for him — one even gives him Chinese-style massages. Combs has spent thousands of dollars in the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside the facility to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him. A spokesperson for the disgraced hip-hop mogul downplayed the details, saying “the only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.” But photos and videos taken from inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News paint a picture of wealth, even behind bars. Read more on our exclusive look inside Combs’ experience in prison. Israel-bound flight diverted amid reports that a pilot was stabbed in the cockpit A flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia amid reports of a bloody onboard altercation. The mother of a passenger on the FlyDubai plane said her daughter heard screaming and somebody, whom she believed was a pilot, asking for help. She said the plane started to lose control, with one man taking out a knife and attempting to kill the pilot. “There was a lot of blood around,” she said, according to her daughter’s account. The Israeli military told NBC News that the country had scrambled at least two jets in response to the incident. They said the military had not yet ruled out the possibility of the incident being terrorism-related. Read more about the emergency landing. Settlers clash with Israeli forces to prevent Palestinian family’s return to West Bank home The Tubassi family was forced to leave their home in July after a siege by violent Jewish settlers in the West Bank town of Jalud, but after Israeli forces tried to facilitate their return, they were met with more violence. Mahmoud Tubassi said he was told that Israeli officials would accompany him, his wife and their son, but settlers started throwing stones at the armed police and military when they arrived at their home. After the settlers entered the property, the family was urged by the security forces to go to the roof. The soldiers formed a physical barrier between the family and the settlers, Tubassi said. The family were then told to get back in an armored car and driven to safety, he added. It was the second time Tubassi and his wife Aida Ahmed Abdullah suffered at the hands of settlers. On Aug. 28, a group attacked them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them. Though the family’s repeated attempts to return home are the result of an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice, the attacks have become a growing concern for the country’s leaders, who have struggled to explain how such a formidable military has found itself outmatched by hundreds of lightly armed young men. That’s the story I heard from seven anguished members of The Buckingham Continuing Care Community in Houston, TX. articles.title: Harry and Meghan blame ‘extraordinarily reckless’ paparazzi for security scare at children’s school
articles.summary: Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex have condemned what they described as “extraordinarily reckless” behavior by international photographers who they say sparked a security scare at their children’s school.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex have condemned what they described as “extraordinarily reckless” behavior by international photographers who they say sparked a security scare at their children’s school. Private security and school staff are understood to have spotted two young men carrying backpacks, later identified as international photographers, walking around the school and stopping to look into the grounds. A spokesperson for the Sussexes called it “an extraordinary lack of judgment” and an “unacceptable intrusion” after the photographers were seen “walking the perimeter of the school.” “It is concerning enough that certain European paparazzi appear unwilling to respect the privacy of children at school,” the spokesperson said. “But to behave in this manner in these particular circumstances, and so soon after the incident at RAF Fairford, demonstrates an extraordinary lack of judgment.” The spokesperson continued, “Whatever photographs they may have been seeking, this was not only an unacceptable intrusion into the privacy of children; it was an irresponsible and ill-considered way to conduct themselves in the vicinity of a school.” CNN has reached out to police for comment. British media outlets have taken care not to identify the location of the school or the Sussexes’ residence following a request from the Independent Press Standards Organisation, though their rules do not apply to representatives working for international media outlets. Prince Harry has long expressed concerns over his family’s security, even before they returned to the UK in late August. Earlier this month, they moved Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, from a previous school just days into the start of the academic term due to security practicalities. When Harry and Meghan stepped back from royal duties in 2020, the British government decided to downgrade their level of taxpayer-funded security – a decision which the duke fought unsuccessfully in the courts for years. In one of those rulings, the UK’s Home Office argued it was not appropriate for wealthy individuals to buy protective security from specialist police officers. Harry has continued pressing for protection, often drawing comparisons of what his wife has faced with that of his mother, Diana, who died in 1997 in a high-speed car crash while paparazzi were following her. This latest incident comes as the couple are reportedly waiting on an official risk assessment now they have returned to the UK from Montecito, California. The couple has been asked to provide authorities with as much detail as possible about their new daily routines, including trips such as the school run, addresses routinely visited, routes taken and more, according to The Telegraph newspaper earlier this month. That information, along with any other evidence considered relevant, will be used by a branch of the UK’s Home Office to evaluate any changes to the level of threat they face.

articles.title: Meet Serge Boghossian, the 16-year-old Canadian student who taught himself to code and built a job platform; hundreds of teens have already joined
articles.summary: 16-year-old Serge Boghossian has turned a problem he faced while looking for work into a platform designed to help other teenagers find their first jobs.
articles.body: 16-year-old Serge Boghossian has turned a problem he faced while looking for work into a platform designed to help other teenagers find their first jobs. The Mississauga student taught himself to code and built Jobbli, a free online service connecting local teenagers with businesses offering part-time work. The idea came from seeing friends struggle to find employment and from his own difficulty getting a first opportunity. What began as a small project has since developed into a platform that Boghossian hopes can eventually reach young job seekers beyond his home city.Serge Boghossian from Canada build a job platform for teenagersBoghossian was born and raised in Mississauga and began working on Jobbli after noticing how difficult it could be for teenagers to enter the job market. Modern Mississauga reported that the idea came to him in November 2025 after watching friends struggle to find their first jobs. He spent about 2 weeks researching and planning before writing his first line of code.The rest of the process was largely self-directed. According to The Pointer, Boghossian had no mentor or school programme teaching him how to code, and he did not rely on his parents to build the platform. Instead, he learnt through YouTube tutorials and continued working on his skills until he could create the service himself.Before Jobbli, he had already built a messaging platform using HTML and JavaScript. That earlier project gave him experience that he later used to create the more complex job platform, The Pointer reported.Need of a separate platform for young job seekersJobbli was created around a straightforward gap in the employment market. Modern Mississauga described it as a free, local platform for Mississauga teenagers aged 14 to 17 who are looking for part-time work. The publication reported that many mainstream job sites are designed with adults in mind, while listings suitable for younger workers can be scattered across social media, word of mouth and community noticeboards.Boghossian also noticed that local businesses faced the opposite problem. Restaurants, tutoring centres, banquet halls and gyms could be interested in hiring teenagers but did not always have an easy way to reach them. Jobbli was designed to bring both sides together in one place.The Pointer reported that Boghossian wanted the platform to be easy for teenagers to use, instead of expecting them to have professional qualifications or years of experience. Teens can look for opportunities, apply and communicate with employers through the platform.Challenges faced by Serge while developing JobbliCreating the technology was only part of the challenge. Modern Mississauga reported that Boghossian found being taken seriously at 16 difficult, particularly when speaking directly with restaurant owners and local organisations. He had to demonstrate that the project was more than a school experiment.The business side also required him to learn skills that were not part of coding. He had to work out how to approach employers, explain the idea and follow up when businesses did not respond positively. Building the platform alone also meant spending long hours fixing problems in his own code without a senior developer to turn to, according to Modern Mississauga.His first step towards wider local recognition came when he contacted the Cooksville Business Improvement Area(BIA) himself. The Pointer reported that he cold-called the organisation to ask whether it could help promote Jobbli and later met with the BIA in person.How does Jobbli handle the needs of teenage usersBecause the platform is intended for teenagers, Boghossian has placed particular attention on privacy and safety. The Pointer reported that Jobbli uses Supabase for built-in security features, including measures intended to reduce the risk of employers sending harmful links to young job seekers.That concern is particularly important because the platform deals with minors. Boghossian said the privacy layer was intended to make teenagers less vulnerable while communicating with employers.Modern Mississauga also reported that employers can post jobs for free, while teenagers can apply, message employers and arrange interviews through the same platform. The aim is to make the process less scattered than the traditional search for a first job.What happened after the first version was releasedBoghossian did not wait until Jobbli was completely polished before allowing people to use it. The Pointer reported that he released Version 1.0 to gather feedback and see whether teenagers would engage with the idea.That early release helped him improve the platform before trying to reach a wider audience. Modern Mississauga reported that his first version was not perfect, but getting it into the hands of real users allowed him to begin conversations with employers rather than continuing to work on it privately.The response from teenagers and parents was described as particularly encouraging as per Modern Mississauga, although Boghossian said employers needed more convincing before trying something new. The Pointer reported that he was also in early discussions with myBlueprint, a Canadian education and career planning platform used by students and parents.How Boghossian plans to expand JobbliFor now, the focus remains on Mississauga. The Pointer reported that Boghossian's immediate task is to persuade more local employers to use the platform while attracting teenagers to it. Modern Mississauga reported that Boghossian wants other young entrepreneurs to build something for a community they understand personally. His own experience as a Mississauga teenager helped him recognise a problem among people his age and shape a tool around it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine’s Kyiv region kill four, target power grid
articles.summary: City officials say three killed in Ukraine’s capital, as emergency services say child killed in the surrounding region.
articles.body:
Russian attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region have killed at least four people, including a child, Ukrainian officials said, as Moscow presses on with its weeks-long bombardment of the Ukrainian capital.

The overnight barrage into Wednesday targeted energy facilities, damaging the power grid and disrupting electricity supplies in and around the Ukrainian capital, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had struck power infrastructure in the Kyiv region.

DTEK, a major private Ukrainian energy company, said crews had restored electricity to about 8,000 households after the attacks. The company said parts of the grid had been damaged, adding to pressure on an energy system repeatedly hit during the war.

Kyiv was under air alerts for much of the night as missiles and drones approached the city. Ukrainian officials reported damage to homes, businesses, warehouses and vehicles.

Kyiv officials reported three deaths in the capital, while emergency services said a child was killed in the surrounding region.

Zelenskyy said critical infrastructure was also struck in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its overnight operation used missiles and drones and included attacks on energy facilities in the Kyiv region that it said were connected to Ukrainian military production.

Moscow also said it struck a communications facility in Kyiv and port infrastructure in the southern city of Izmail.

The attack followed several days of heavier pressure on Kyiv, including strikes during daylight hours as well as repeated overnight barrages.

Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered attack drones that travel faster than earlier models and are harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept.

That challenge has added urgency to Ukraine’s calls for more air-defence support from its allies, particularly interceptors capable of countering ballistic missiles.

Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken warned in Brussels on Wednesday that Europe could face more Russian “hybrid threats” in the coming months.

Francken called for faster expansion of air defences, weapons stocks and production.

The attacks come as temperatures begin to fall ahead of the winter months.

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy system during the previous winter caused electricity and heating outages during severe cold, leaving the condition of the power network a major concern as the country heads towards another winter of war.

articles.title: Money the ‘root cause’ behind Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi’s murder, prosecutors say
articles.summary: A family dispute over money was the “root cause” that motivated the killing and dismemberment of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi, prosecutors told a court Wednesday, as the trial of her ex-husband and in-laws accused of murdering her began.
articles.body: A family dispute over money was the “root cause” that motivated the killing and dismemberment of Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi, prosecutors told a court Wednesday, as the trial of her ex-husband and in-laws accused of murdering her began. The gruesome 2023 murder of Choi, who rubbed shoulders with showbiz elites at fashion events and had a significant following online, sent shockwaves through the wealthy financial hub and made global headlines. Police at the time revealed only parts of Choi’s body had been located, deepening the intense media reporting - and social media speculation - over why the life of a popular socialite had been cut short so violently. Her ex-husband Alex Kwong, his brother Anothy Kwong and their father Kwong Kau are on trial for her killing. All three officially pleaded not guilty to her murder on Wednesday. In her opening speech, prosecutor Charlotte Draycott highlighted the significant difference in wealth between Choi and her former in-laws, describing how arguments over finances and her plans to sell a luxury apartment set in motion what became a family plot to murder her. “Money seems to be to root cause of this case,” Draycott told the jury of eight men and one woman. Choi was no longer married to Alex Kwong by the time of her murder and her new partner hailed from an “extremely wealthy” family. But Choi remained in contact with the Kwong family, who Dracott said “were not rich people,” and helped financially support them. After separating with her ex-husband, Draycott said, Choi continued to provide “generous allowance” to the Kwongs, including a HK$60 million ($7.6 million) apartment under Kwong Kau’s name, in part because they helped take care of her two children with Alex Kwong. The once cordial relationship with Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, turned soar in 2022 when she tried to sell the luxuriously renovated apartment, and move her in-laws to an area further away from downtown where her children could go to school, according to Draycott. Tensions spiraled in the months leading up to her murder. Kwong Kau came to disown Choi and allegedly tried to assault her on one occasion, Draycott said. Choi was also angry, describing her ex-father-in-law as a “crook” and “ungrateful” as she grew increasingly worried that the Kwongs would turn her children against her. Draycott said Kwong Kau eventually plotted to murder Choi. “If she died, the flat would be in his name and he could move back there,” Draycott said. “He made a plan with his two sons Alex, her ex-husband, and Anthony, and we say three of them decided they would do it together,” she told the jurors. “Each of them played a part by bringing her death and burying her body.” Police previously said Choi - a mother of four, including two children with her ex-husband Alex Kwong - went missing on February 21, 2023. Three days later, body parts believed to be hers were recovered at a house in the city’s Tai Po district, where police also found a meat slicer, an electric saw, and some clothing. The Kwongs were arrested soon after. On Wednesday, the jury also heard Choi was born on the southern Chinese island of Hainan and moved to Hong Kong at the age of five. She met Alex Kwong when she was still in school and the pair got married in 2014. During her marriage, Alex Kwong never had a job and depended on Choi’s family to support them, Draycott said. The trial continues Friday and is expected to last at least eight weeks.

articles.title: Swinney to introduce misogyny education in every school in Scotland
articles.summary: The first minister says he wants to challenge misogynistic behaviour in young boys and strengthen and support young girls.
articles.body:
John Swinney has vowed to introduce programmes to educate pupils about misogyny in every school in Scotland.

The first minister said violence against women and girls was of "such seismic significance" that it made the move necessary.

He has previously described the situation as a "national emergency" with Police Scotland saying more than 200 crimes of violence against women and girls are recorded on average every day.

Swinney said Scotland's education system must be a primary focus to challenge misogynistic behaviour in young boys - and give young girls "the strength and resilience to say, that's not acceptable".

The first minister told BBC Radio Scotland's Mornings programme : "We've been working over the summer on what I would call preventative interventions.

"These are education programmes and awareness campaigns which are going to be focused on changing the culture of Scottish society.

"Our education system is going to be a primary focus for that, to make sure that boys are educated and supported to understand the implications of what some might think of as casual behaviour, but it has consequences."

He added: "I'm going to make sure that every school in the country is educating young boys about the dangers and risks of misogyny."

Swinney calls violence against women a 'national emergency' as new advert launched

New adverts urge boys not to share sexist content online

Earlier this year, the Scottish government launched an advertising campaign urging boys and young men not to share misogynistic content online.

The adverts warned boys that sexist content is "never harmless" and has the potential to hurt girls, including people they know.

Swinney said the fact that Scotland doesn't have a mandatory education system had meant that some schools had been tackling the issue more vigorously than others.

"I'm going to address that," he told told Mornings presenter Connie McLaughlin.

"We have got to get alignment between the government and our local authority partners.

"We've got to make sure that's present in every single school in the country."

The first minister said there continued to be debate over the age at which young pupils were introduced to violence-awareness programmes.

"I was criticised heavily when I was education secretary (five years ago) about putting in place materials which were educating young people about concepts such as consent in relationships," he said.

"Some people viewed that it was far too early for that to be undertaken.

"My view was that it was necessary. I think that is inescapable now."

During an hour-long radio phone-in, Swinney said he was "terrified" by the influence of toxic masculinity on young boys and teenagers and was talking to the UK government about tougher online regulations.

He also said he was looking at providing emergency funding for organisations which were struggling to help victims of domestic violence because of long waiting lists.

The first minister was challenged over bail tests by the family of Stacy Hunter, who was murdered at her home near Houston by her estranged husband while he was on bail.

Stacy's brother Sean and their mother Ann have supported calls for a dedicated GPS electronic monitoring scheme for domestic abuse perpetrators who are assessed as posing a significant risk to a partner or former partner.

Earlier this month Swinney announced that, before recess in October, regulations would be lodged to enable the piloting of GPS monitoring for individuals on bail, including those suspected of domestic abuse.

Sean Hunter welcomed news about the GPS tracking but raised concerns about whether the bail system was tight enough.

He said: "We don't want this (GPS tracking) to be used as a tool to release more dangerous people because they'll be tagged."

The first minister said he believed Scotland had a "very strong bail test" which took into account the perspective of victims and the issue of public safety.

However, he said "tragically, there were cases where the judgment was wrong", as in the case of Stacy.

Swinney said the GPS pilot would start in the Tayside and Fife areas.

He added that if the Scottish government was confident in the system, he hoped to see the initiative rolled out as widely and as quickly as possible.
